title: Refused as Insolvent on the 9th, Suspended at 15.30 on the 10th, No Representation Until Two Hours Ago on the 11th
participants: The Chancellor of the Exchequer (not named in Hansard)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: A discount house standing between the Bank of England and the market, earning on paper it did not hold to maturity — and, by the Bank's own later account, not merely short of cash: "On 9 May 1866, Overend Gurney asked the Bank of England for assistance, which was refused on the basis of the broker's insolvency". Two days later the Bank "extended its loans and discounts to-day to a sum of something more than £4,000,000" to everyone else.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural fact is in the Bank's balance sheet as the Chancellor reported it to the House: "we find the Bank reserves reduced in a single day from a sum approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000." Half the reserve of the country's central bank went in one day, under a statute — the Bank Charter Act 1844 — that fixed a limit the Bank was now about to exceed. The Bank's own Bulletin puts it that it "extended the largest market-wide lending it had ever done and drew heavily on its own reserves."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is visible in the question rather than the answer. Mr Disraeli rose to ask "Whether there is any truth in the prevalent rumour that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any relaxation of the provisions of the Bank Charter regulating the issue of notes?" — a rumour was circulating in the City about a government decision the Chancellor then stated had not been taken. Meanwhile the Chancellor told the House he was "not yet cognizant of the actual state of affairs in the City, as it is exhibited from time to time by the accounts of the Bank of England": the minister deciding was behind the market he was deciding about. And the firm itself is nowhere in Hansard — the Chancellor says only "the calamitous event announced yesterday". It is the Bank's Bulletin that names it and times it: suspended "at 15.30 on 10 May 1866".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was an indemnity, granted the same evening and addressed to one institution. The Government determined "to address a letter to the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank" recommending that if the Bank found occasion "to make such advances from the Issue Department as shall exceed the limits allowed by law", it "should not hesitate to make that issue", with the Government undertaking "to make immediate application to Parliament to sanction that proceeding". The statutory limit was set aside by letter, with retrospective parliamentary cover promised — for a Bank that had refused the one house that asked, and was lending record sums to everyone around it.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no inquiry in this record to whitewash anything — the containment is in the diagnosis offered to the House on the night, and in the doctrine the episode hardened into. The uneasiness, the Chancellor said, "does not arise from any general unsoundness in the condition of our commercial relations, but only from causes of a peculiar and specific character." A systemic event was characterised, within hours and before any investigation, as a local and specific one. The rule that grew from it is the one Bordo restates: "The classic prescription for LLR action is to lend freely but at a penalty rate to illiquid but solvent banks. Both Thornton and Bagehot advised strongly against bailouts — assistance to insolvent" institutions. The refusal of one house and the rescue of the market became, afterwards, the correct thing to have done.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Bank Charter Act 1844, and two existing precedents for suspending it — the letters of 1847 and 1857, which the Chancellor cited by date as the model for what he was about to do. Beneath that, a private Bank of England already acting as the market's banker without any stated obligation to do so.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A third letter on the same terms, which is what turns two exceptions into a standing practice — the Chancellor's own words make the inheritance explicit: "substantially the same as was addressed to those high officers in 1847 and 1857" — and a lender-of-last-resort rule that draws its line at solvency: free lending at a penalty rate to the illiquid, nothing for the insolvent.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The Bank lends to sustain commerce; lending drains the reserve; the drained reserve is the reason the statutory limit must be lifted; lifting the limit lets the lending continue. Each turn of the loop is also the precedent for the next, which is why there was a form of words ready in 1866 — and refusing one insolvent house while carrying every solvent counterparty around it converts a private bank's discretion into a standing public expectation.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Two opposite decoys share this dossier. One: that the Government and the Bank had the rescue prepared in advance — that insiders knew the crash was coming and the suspension of the Bank Charter Act was the payoff arranged beforehand. The other: that the Bank of England let Overend Gurney fail because it would not intervene in the market at all.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The first fails on the best available evidence against it, which is the Chancellor's own account under hostile questioning from Disraeli in the same sitting: "no truth" in the rumour of a decision, "they have not arrived at any decision", "until two hours or two hours and a half ago no representation or formal report of any kind had reached me from the City", and — hardest to reconcile with a prepared plan — "I have not the least reason to suppose that any request from that quarter", the Bank's directors, "is likely to reach the Government." Later the same evening: "the extraordinary rapidity with which the crisis has come upon us, and which has reduced the opportunity of deliberation given to the Government within very narrow limits indeed." A minister can lie to the House, and this dossier cannot exclude it; but the version the record supports is that there was no plan, there was a form of words from 1847 and 1857, and an afternoon was enough. What the record DOES show is who moved it: "gentlemen representing in particular the private banks of London" came first, then "a deputation regularly constituted from the joint-stock banks in London", pressing "even more earnestly and urgently than I anticipated". The second decoy fails on the Bank's own account. It did refuse Overend Gurney, on 9 May, "on the basis of the broker's insolvency" — and then "extended the largest market-wide lending it had ever done and drew heavily on its own reserves." Its restraint was aimed at a single counterparty, not at the market. The two sources were read by two different sessions working from different bases — Hansard here, the Bank's 2016 Bulletin and Bordo on a parallel branch, verified there and carried in at the merge with that stated — and they agree on the one point that matters: the house was refused, and the market around it was carried, within a day.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Two exchanges in the House of Commons on 11 May 1866, printed in Hansard at vol 183 cc772-4 and cc840-2. In the first, the Chancellor of the Exchequer states that no decision has been taken, that no representation had reached him until two to two and a half hours earlier, that he has since received an "important requisition" and seen "many of the most influential and respected members of the body of the London bankers" with a joint-stock bank deputation expected, that those bankers describe the panic as "without parallel in the recollection of the oldest men of business in the City of London" and "suggest and desire that in some form or other relief should be afforded", and that he has no reason to expect any request from the Bank of England's directors. In the second, hours later, he reports that the Bank has lent more than £4,000,000 that day, that its reserves fell in a single day from approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000, and that the Government has determined to send the Governor and Deputy Governor a letter substantially the same as those of 1847 and 1857, authorising issue beyond the legal limit with a promise of retrospective parliamentary sanction. He attributes the crisis not to "any general unsoundness" but to "causes of a peculiar and specific character", and notes the extraordinary rapidity with which it arrived. Neither debate names the failed firm. The Bank of England's Quarterly Bulletin of 2016 Q2, as read and verified on a parallel branch, names it and dates it: on 9 May 1866 Overend Gurney asked the Bank for assistance and was refused on the basis of insolvency; it suspended payments at 15.30 on 10 May 1866; and the Bank, a private bank at the time, extended the largest market-wide lending it had ever done and drew heavily on its own reserves. Bordo's NBER paper, read on the same branch, states the doctrine that followed: lend freely at a penalty rate to the illiquid but solvent, and nothing for the insolvent, as both Thornton and Bagehot advised. The letter itself, the Bank's 1866 records, and any account of who gained or lost were not read.

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE PANIC IN THE CITY" — QUESTION, HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc772-4 (Historic Hansard, 1803–2005)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. (The URL slug is "question-5" because the service names child items of a debate heading by position; it is reached from the sitting index for 11 May 1866 and the page header reads "THE PANIC IN THE CITY. / QUESTION. / HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc772-4".) THE FIRM IS NOT NAMED. Nowhere in this exchange, or in the Bank Charter Act exchange later the same evening, does the word "Overend" appear; the Chancellor refers only to "the calamitous event announced yesterday". This dossier therefore takes the identification of the failed house from its own title and not from this document. WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS. MR. DISRAELI opened: "I take this opportunity of inquiring of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Whether there is any truth in the prevalent rumour that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any relaxation of the provisions of the Bank Charter regulating the issue of notes?" MR. BAZLEY and MR. BIDDULPH pressed the same point, Mr Biddulph asking "whether he is prepared to relax the provisions of the Bank Act in the event of the Bank directors making a proposition to that effect". THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER replied — and his answer is a timeline given under questioning: "there is no truth in the statement that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any step to be taken at variance with the provisions of the Act of 1844. In point of fact, they have not arrived at any decision upon the subject of the state of things which prevails in the City in immediate connection with the calamitous event announced yesterday. I may go further and say, that until two hours or two hours and a half ago no representation or formal report of any kind had reached me from the City upon the subject of the existing state of things; but for the last two hours and a half my time has been occupied in receiving information and statements, and, I may add, an important requisition from very influential persons connected with the City." ON WHO CAME: "I have seen many of the most influential and respected members of the body of the London bankers on the subject, and I have not yet had time to see, but I expect to see as soon as my engagements in this House will allow me to leave my place, a deputation regularly constituted from the joint-stock banks in London to the same effect." ON WHAT THEY SAID: "The purport of the statements made by them is that they conceive the state of panic and distress which prevails in the City to be without parallel in the recollection of the oldest men of business in the City of London. They suggest and desire that in some form or other relief should be afforded." ON THE BANK OF ENGLAND, which had not asked: "The hon. Gentleman behind me has asked me whether we should consent to suspend the Bank Act in the event of the Directors of the Bank of England making a proposition to that effect. On that question I should wish to make this remark: in the first place, having stated our anxiety to proceed promptly with this matter, I think I had better not answer any question; especially any question relating to the hypothesis of a request by the Directors of the Bank of England, for I have not the least reason to suppose that any request from that quarter is likely to reach the Government." He also described the Bank as "the mirror of the monetary" state "of the country". THE SPEAKER IS NOT NAMED IN THE RECORD: Hansard identifies him only as "THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER", and this dossier does not name the individual, because this page does not. TRANSCRIPTION FAULTS IN THE DIGITISED TEXT, recorded so that nothing is quoted from them: the passage about the Bank reads "the mirror of the monetary slate of the country" and "from the the actual trans actions of the Bank" — "slate" for "state" and a split word, which are artefacts of the digitisation, not of the 1866 text. Quotations above avoid those phrases or mark the substitution.

citations.title: House of Commons, "SUSPENSION OF THE BANK CHARTER ACT." — QUESTION, HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc840-2 (Historic Hansard, 1803–2005)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. This is the SAME SITTING as the "Panic in the City" exchange, some hours later — the two are the morning and the evening of 11 May 1866, and read together they are a decision being taken inside a single afternoon. MR. BAZLEY asked "Whether he has consented to recommend any peculiar facilities to be extended to the Bank of England during the existing monetary panic". THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER answered: "I stated, in the commencement of the evening, that representations had been made to me from quarters of the greatest influence and credit with respect to the extraordinary state of alarm and distress prevailing in the City to-day. I stated that those representations had come to me from gentlemen representing in particular the private banks of London, and I expected that I should shortly receive similar representations from those connected with the joint-stock banks. Those representations I have received accordingly, and they were pressed even more earnestly and urgently than I anticipated." THE NUMBERS THE GOVERNMENT ACTED ON: "we find that the Bank, moved by a just desire to sustain the commerce of the country, and to avert disaster, has extended its loans and discounts to-day to a sum of something more than £4,000,000. The effect of that large accommodation was to reduce the reserves of the Bank to a sum not very far short of £3,000,000 of money" — and, stated again, "we find the Bank reserves reduced in a single day from a sum approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000." THE DECISION, AND ITS PRECEDENT: "we have determined to address a letter to the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank, substantially the same as was addressed to those high officers in 1847 and 1857. That is to say, if the Bank, proceeding upon its usual prudent rules of administration, shall find occasion, in order to meet the wants of legitimate commerce, to make such advances from the Issue Department as shall exceed the limits allowed by law, we recommend that they should not hesitate to make that issue, and we undertake, in the event of the arrival of that contingency, to make immediate application to Parliament to sanction that proceeding." ON HOW LITTLE TIME THERE WAS — the sentence that bears directly on any claim of a prepared plan: "there is also another distinction, and that is the extraordinary rapidity with which the crisis has come upon us, and which has reduced the opportunity of deliberation given to the Government within very narrow limits indeed. We have not, however, hesitated to act". ON THE DIAGNOSIS OFFERED TO THE HOUSE: the uneasiness "does not arise from any general unsoundness in the condition of our commercial relations, but only from causes of a peculiar and specific character." WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT CONTAIN: the letter itself (promised "in the hands of the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank to-morrow") was not read; no Bank of England record was read; the failed house is never named; and there is nothing here about who profited, who was ruined, or what any private party knew in advance.
